video_title: Coldcard Hackers Are Still Draining Bitcoin Wallets Right Now. What You Need to Know
gist: Galaxy Digital's head of firmwide research, Alex Thorn, walks through his on-chain forensics of the Coldcard/Coinkite weak-entropy exploit: 8,300 addresses and 1,720 BTC (~$112M) confirmed stolen as of August 10, with ~92% of the coins sitting unmoved in attacker addresses. He argues Coinkite's shift away from fully open source and hostility to vulnerability reporters left the bug undetected for five years, describes a 25-person volunteer red team scanning 500+ Bitcoin repos with AI (forced onto Chinese open-source models because US frontier models block cyber work), and quantifies the self-custody fallout, including ~30,000 BTC flowing into exchanges since the event. He closes on the failed BIP 110 fork.

themes.theme: Coldcard exploit scope and victim-report forensics

insights.claim: As of August 10, 2026, Galaxy Digital's Alex Thorn has high-confidence attribution of 8,300 Bitcoin addresses drained via the Coldcard/Coinkite entropy exploit, totaling 1,720 BTC worth roughly $112 million, with additional unconfirmed patterns that could push the total to about 2,100 BTC.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Sets the hard upper bound on realized losses so far and flags that the confirmed number is still rising as more victims report.
insights.quote: 8,300 addresses worth 1,720 Bitcoin uh worth about $112 million at this moment as we record on Monday, August 10th.

insights.claim: Because the stolen Bitcoin originates in thousands of unconnected individual wallets rather than one centralized honeypot, tracing runs backwards from victim reports rather than forward from a breach point, which is why Thorn has had to catalog 29 additional attack patterns (labeled footprints A through AC) beyond the three original waves.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Explains why reported loss figures will keep climbing and why blockchain-analytics vendors cannot size this event the way they size an exchange hack.

insights.claim: Engineers at Block Inc. flagged the first burst of suspicious transactions on July 31, 2026, one day after Coinkite published its initial security advisory around 6-7pm Eastern on July 30, and that pattern became the basis for what analysts now call wave one.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Establishes the disclosure-to-exploitation timeline, which matters for any liability or insurance analysis of Coinkite.

insights.claim: Losses skew toward ordinary savers rather than large holders: the median loss per address is 0.014 BTC and the mean 0.212 BTC, while across the 130-plus victims Thorn has corresponded with directly the median loss is 1 BTC and the mean is 4 BTC.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: The victim base is retail self-custodians, so the reputational damage to hardware-wallet self-custody exceeds the dollar size of the theft.
insights.quote: by victim, the median loss is one Bitcoin and the mean loss is four Bitcoin

insights.claim: The average dormancy of the stolen coins is roughly four years, meaning the victims are long-term savers who did nothing speculative, not recent buyers or DeFi yield chasers.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Confirms that genuinely dormant, high-conviction supply is being forced into motion, and that the emotional damage lands on the most committed cohort of holders.
insights.quote: The reality is these people did everything right.

themes.theme: Attacker behavior and odds of recovery

insights.claim: Roughly 1,500 of the 1,700 confirmed-stolen BTC, about 92%, are sitting inert in second-hop attacker addresses and have not moved since the late-July thefts, with only smaller footprints showing bridging to other networks or deposits at offshore casinos.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: The stolen supply is not being dumped, so there is no immediate sell-side overhang, but a future move by these addresses would be a watchable on-chain event.
insights.quote: 1,500 or more of the 1,700 that I'm tracking are sitting in there 92% of the ones that have been taken confirmed taken with high confidence.

insights.claim: Wave three uses a fundamentally different fund-flow topography from waves one and two, segregating each victim's coins into their own holding addresses across roughly 285 to 293 attacker addresses, which leads Thorn to suspect a second distinct threat actor.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Multiple independent actors means law enforcement success against one attacker would not recover the bulk of funds.

insights.claim: Thorn expects the large wave one through three holders may sit on the coins for years, citing the Bitfinex hacker who held billions in Bitcoin for about five years before being caught after spending some on Walmart gift cards.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations that recovery, if it comes, is a multi-year law-enforcement outcome, not a near-term event.
insights.quote: the Bitfinex hacker sat on billions of dollars of Bitcoin for like five years before they screwed up and spent a bit of it, I believe, on Walmart gift cards and ultimately got caught

insights.claim: Very few of the stolen coins have gone through CoinJoin, and even those that did remain traceable by timing and amount matching, while exchanges and brokerages routinely flag or freeze coins with CoinJoin history.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Laundering capacity for a theft this size is thin, which raises the odds that any attempt to liquidate leaves an actionable trail.

insights.claim: Block Inc. engineers publicly reported that the wave one attacker used a paid account at a hosted blockchain-data API provider to query the addresses they later stole from, which Thorn considers the strongest existing lead toward identification.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: A KYC'd payment trail at a data vendor is the kind of off-chain footprint that historically resolves these cases, making attribution more likely than the on-chain silence suggests.

insights.claim: Victims will lose the ability to prove ownership cryptographically because the attackers now hold their private keys, and Thorn expects a public GitHub dataset of every vulnerable address and its private key within a few months, so victims must formally establish victimhood now via FBI IC3 or Canada's RCMP reports.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: The window to establish a recoverable claim is closing; filing early is the only mechanism that converts a frozen or white-hat-recovered coin into a returned coin.
insights.quote: I would expect within a few months there's, like, the list of every single vulnerable address and its private key will be a public data set you can see on GitHub.

themes.theme: Root cause: closed-off code and thin auditing

insights.claim: Thorn attributes the entropy bug to Coinkite moving its free and open-source code into a semi-open-source license out of anger that another project was using it, then behaving combatively toward developers submitting vulnerability reports, which caused outside reviewers to stop examining the codebase.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Licensing posture and developer-community relations are now a measurable security risk factor when evaluating any hardware or infrastructure vendor.
insights.quote: they introduced the bug out of um hubris and anger that uh another project was using their source code

insights.claim: No advanced AI model was required to find the Coldcard bug, because everyone building cryptographic key products knows that sufficient entropy in random number generation is essential; the failure was a lack of eyeballs on the code, and earlier user reports of similar losses had been dismissed by Coinkite years ago.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Reframes the incident from an AI-capability story to a governance and audit-coverage story, which is the risk to screen for across other wallet vendors.
insights.quote: it really I think boils down to a lack of sufficient eyeballs on their code.

insights.claim: Thorn cannot confirm the Chinese open-source model referred to as Kimmy K3 discovered the bug but notes the timing lines up and that open-source models lack the cyber safeguards US frontier models impose, and he does believe AI was used heavily by the first three wave attackers to operationalize the attack.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Signals that AI-assisted exploitation of legacy cryptographic bugs is now operational, raising the expected rate of similar events across older codebases.

insights.claim: There is no remediation path for a bug in already-generated seeds: a firmware update cannot fix keys already created, the user must move funds manually, and any mass warning immediately tips off attackers, a problem compounded by Coinkite's policy of deleting customer data to avoid creating a home-address honeypot for physical attackers.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: The privacy practice buyers valued most became the reason the vendor could not warn them, a structural tradeoff that applies to every privacy-first hardware vendor.

themes.theme: Volunteer red team and AI-policy friction

insights.claim: A volunteer red team of roughly 25 people led by Rob Hamilton in Nashville, with Calle from Cashu and James O'Byrne, has spent about ten days comprehensively auditing open-source Bitcoin software, scanning just over 500 repositories with as many as 100 running in parallel on a bare-metal server and responsibly disclosing findings.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: A wave of AI-assisted disclosures across Bitcoin tooling is likely in coming weeks, so expect further vendor advisories independent of Coldcard.
insights.quote: you say don't trust, verify? Well, Coldcard shows we weren't quite verifying, certainly not enough.

insights.claim: The headline positive finding from the audit sweep is that libsecp256k1, the library doing signature math for essentially all of Bitcoin, came back clean after dozens of hours of adversarial testing, with no evidence of a problem in Bitcoin itself.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Contains the blast radius to vendor implementations rather than the protocol, which is the distinction that determines whether this is an idiosyncratic or systemic event.
insights.quote: libsec P256K1, which is the um, does the signature math for basically all of Bitcoin, um, came back with no no bugs after dozens of hours of trying to break it.

insights.claim: US frontier AI models block the red team's vulnerability-finding work, forcing defenders onto Chinese open-source models even when a participant like Rob Hamilton holds a security clearance, which Thorn and Brunell both frame as a national-security policy failure.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Points to a live policy gap and a demand pocket for cyber-defense-permitted model access; also an argument for open-weight model adoption in security tooling.
insights.quote: there's no reason why American companies and individuals should have to be relying on Chinese AI in order to defend themselves from cyberattacks.

insights.claim: Thorn argues other crypto networks should run equivalent AI-assisted audits and are better funded to do so through ICO or pre-mine foundation treasuries, whereas Bitcoin's effort has been unfunded volunteer work sustained partly by donations covering AI token spend.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Flags latent, unaudited vulnerability risk across altcoin wallet and library stacks that have not yet run this exercise.

insights.claim: Roughly 30,000 BTC has flowed into exchanges since the Coldcard event according to Sunny from Time Chain Index, and CryptoQuant published a chart showing one of the largest spikes in sub-1 BTC deposits to exchanges in a long time, a dynamic one observer labeled the reverse FTX.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: A measurable reversal of the post-FTX self-custody trend; rising exchange balances from small holders is a flow signal to track alongside price.
insights.quote: somebody called it the reverse FTX, you know, after FTX collapsed, like funds flowed out of exchanges all around the world into self-custody because people were worried there'd be another FTX

insights.claim: Only single-sig Coldcard setups where the user did not supply their own entropy are affected, and Thorn urges anyone who does not remember rolling dice 100 times or generating a strong passphrase to move funds immediately, using a regulated venue like River as a temporary destination if no better setup exists.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: A concrete triage rule that determines whether a holder faces certain loss or no exposure at all.
insights.quote: if you're not on a single sig cold card setup, like you are not affected by this vulnerability, to be clear.

insights.claim: Multi-sig users holding one vulnerable Coldcard among independent keys remain safe because a cracked key cannot reach signing quorum, and Thorn has not yet found a single instance of a multi-sig being drained, though two vulnerable Coldcards in a 2-of-3 would eventually be exposed.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Empirical validation that key-diversified multi-sig contains single-vendor implementation failures, which strengthens the case for multi-vendor custody products.

insights.claim: Thorn expects near- and medium-term hesitancy toward self-custody and tells anxious unaffected holders that using a trusted regulated custodian such as Coinbase or River is preferable to hastily rebuilding a self-custody setup, citing people who panicked and lost funds to scam wallets; Trezor and Ledger have published audits stating they are unaffected.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Suggests a durable share shift toward regulated custodians and away from hardware wallets, benefiting exchanges and collaborative-custody providers.

insights.claim: The BIP 110 fork that split off in early August failed exactly as predicted, has substantially less support than prior hostile forks including Bitcoin Cash and probably Bitcoin SV, and its backers are now discussing a new ticker and a changed proof-of-work hashing algorithm, making it effectively a new altcoin.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Removes fork risk as an overhang and sets expectations that any BIP 110 chain token trades as a marginal altcoin rather than a contender.
insights.quote: This fork was destined to fail, and it failed exactly the way like dozens and dozens and dozens of smart Bitcoiners told them it would.

insights.claim: Thorn argues that if Bitcoin could actually be upgraded with the roughly 2.5% of hash rate and 17% of nodes the BIP 110 camp cited, that would be far more bearish for Bitcoin than anything they allege about Bitcoin Core, because a vocal-minority upgrade path is indistinguishable from a bona fide attack.
insights.speaker: Alex Thorn
insights.so_what: Reframes fork resistance as a core value driver of the asset, useful when assessing any future contentious change proposal.
